L01:
FlagShip raised a $4.2M seed round. Basis Ventures led.

We've spent 18 months building a feature-flag platform on one belief: shipping software shouldn't be scary. Flags shouldn't be the thing you bolt on after deploys start going wrong. They should be how you ship in the first place.

We're still a team of 6. The money goes to hiring engineers and to shipping faster for the customers who bet on us early.

If you want to work on developer tools and you have opinions about feature management, my DMs are open.
L02:
Nine months. Three teams. Our monolith is finally gone, and the fintech now runs on microservices.

p99 latency is down 40%. Deploys that took hours now take minutes.

The surprise was that the technical work turned out to be the easy part. Getting three teams to agree on service boundaries, on ownership, and on standards took more energy than any line of code we wrote. If I did it again, I'd start with the domain, not the technology, and I'd migrate in slices. Big-bang rewrites die.

Microservices get called overhyped constantly. Sometimes they're still exactly the right tool. This was one of those times.

What's the longest migration you've lived through?
L03:
We're hiring a founding designer at our AI startup in Austin.

First design hire. You report to the CEO. Equity is 0.5 to 1%, which is real ownership, not a gesture.

There's no design system yet, no brand, no research practice. You'd be building all of it, and you'd be deciding how people interact with AI inside our product, which I think is one of the more interesting design problems going.

You need to be comfortable with ambiguity, because there's plenty. Sweating the details has to be your default setting.

Austin preferred. We'll flex for the right person.

If this is you, or you know exactly who it is, my DMs are open.
L04:
I was laid off from a big tech company in January. Six months later, I'm leading product at a 30-person startup.

The middle was the hardest stretch of my career. 200+ applications. Interviews that went nowhere. Days I questioned what I was worth.

Two things I'd say to anyone in that spot right now. Your job isn't your identity, and I say that as someone who needed most of those six months to believe it. And the silence is worse than the rejections, so to the hiring managers who sent real, thoughtful nos instead of nothing: it mattered more than you know.

New chapter starts now. If you're mid-search and need someone to talk to, my DMs are open.
L05:
Most AI agent startups are thin wrappers around the same 3 foundation models.

I watch the launches every week: a clever prompt, a polished UI, and a foundation model doing all the real work underneath. Prompts are not a moat. Anyone can copy yours in an afternoon, including the model providers themselves.

What holds up is less glamorous. Workflow depth: being wired so far into how a team operates that ripping you out costs more than keeping you. And data: feedback loops that make the product smarter every day in ways a new entrant can't copy.

The winners here won't have the best demos. They'll know their customers' workflows better than the customers do.

If you're building one, the test is simple. If the model providers ship your feature tomorrow, what's left?
L06:
Home from SaaStr Annual. I talked with 40+ founders over the week, and three things kept coming up.

PLG has grown up. Companies aren't treating product-led growth as a religion anymore; the sophisticated ones are layering sales on top of self-serve and feeling no shame about it.

Nobody has cracked AI pricing. Seat-based, usage-based, outcome-based: every founder I asked is running a different experiment, and not one of them sounded confident. That was the most honest thing I heard all week.

Community-led growth is back, and this time it arrives with real ROI expectations attached.

There's more energy in SaaS right now than I've seen in years.

If you were there and left with a different read on pricing, I want to hear it.
L07:
Roughly 70% of enterprise AI pilots never reach production. The models aren't the reason. The models have been ready for a while.

Two things kill pilots.

Data readiness. Most enterprises sit on fragmented, inconsistent, badly governed data, and you can't build production AI on spreadsheets and silos.

Process redesign, or the absence of it. Bolting AI onto an existing workflow and waiting for magic doesn't work; the process itself has to change, and teams that skip that step watch the pilot die in the demo phase.

The companies that make it to production do the unglamorous work first. They clean the data, redesign the process, and prepare people for the change before anyone demos anything.

The bottleneck isn't the technology. We are.
L08:
Clearlens v2 shipped today.

It comes out of 300+ customer interviews over the past year, and the two most requested features got built: session replay, so you can watch exactly how a user moves through your product, and funnel comparison, so you can put two conversion paths side by side and see which one leaks.

14 beta customers spent the past few months testing and breaking both. Their feedback shaped every pixel of this release.

The lesson I keep relearning: customers already know what your roadmap should be. You just have to ask.

This is the biggest release we've shipped. Link's in the first comment if you're curious what your users are really doing inside your product.
L09:
The number one skill in B2B sales, after 10 years of doing it, is listening. Not pitching, not negotiating. Listening.

A few years ago I was on a call with a deal that was falling apart. The prospect had concerns, and every instinct I had said fill the air with answers. Instead I went quiet and stayed quiet. Ninety seconds of silence on a live call. It was excruciating.

Then the prospect talked themselves through their own objection and named the real blocker, one I'd never have guessed. We closed the deal two weeks later.

Prospects will tell you exactly how to sell to them if you let them. A decade in, I still have to remind myself to shut up.
L10:
I'm shutting down Cartful.

Three years, $1.1M raised, 4,000 users, and we never found repeatable revenue. That last clause is the whole story; everything else is detail.

Three things I'd tell a founder starting today.

Users are not customers. We celebrated signups while dodging the harder question of who would pay, and why.

Repeatable revenue beats everything. One-off deals feel like traction and aren't. If you can't describe your sales motion in one sentence, you don't have one.

Runway is for learning, not surviving. We stretched ours to stay alive when we should've spent it finding out the truth faster.

To our investors, our team, and our users: thank you, and I'm sorry we couldn't get there.

On to what's next.
L11:
We stopped doing daily standups a few months ago. My team is 14 engineers; the standup became async written updates, three lines each morning: what you did, what you're doing, what's blocking you.

Meetings dropped by 6 hours a week. Shipping speed didn't change at all.

That second number is the damning one. We deleted a daily ritual and delivery didn't notice, which tells you what the ritual was for. Most standups serve the manager, not the team; a status ritual dressed up as collaboration. The written version beats the meeting anyway. People think before they post. Updates are searchable months later. Time zones stop mattering, and the engineers report fewer interruptions and more deep work.

I won't claim standups are always wrong. But if yours feels like a status meeting, it is one, and your team already knows.

Would yours survive the switch?
L12:
I passed the AWS Solutions Architect Professional exam.

Eleven weeks of studying around a full-time job, and the hardest cert I've attempted.

Five practice exams were the highest-value thing I did. Every one exposed gaps I didn't know I had, and by test day the real thing felt familiar. Consistency mattered almost as much: an hour a day beat cramming eight hours on a Saturday, and hands-on labs made concepts stick where videos never did. I also learned to put study time on the calendar like a meeting, because otherwise the job ate it.

If you're grinding toward a cert while working full-time, it's a slog and it's doable. Protect the hour.

Next step is using the thing.
L13:
A year into being an engineering manager, the hardest adjustment wasn't the one I expected.

It wasn't the meetings or the difficult conversations. It was learning to measure my output by my team's work instead of my personal commits.

For years my sense of progress came from shipping: green squares, merged PRs, something to point at by Friday. Then my output went invisible. A good week now means my 7 direct reports are unblocked and shipping while my own name shows up nowhere, and it took me months to stop feeling like a fraud about that.

What year one taught me: most problems on a team are communication problems in disguise, and clarity is the most useful thing I produce. The urge to jump in and fix things myself never left. I mostly resist it.

If you're a new EM and the identity shift feels wrong, it isn't just you. It took me the full year.
L14:
Our on-call pages dropped 30% in a single quarter. We didn't buy a tool or rebuild a system. We wrote runbooks.

Nine SREs, and until this year too much of our operational knowledge lived only in people's heads. The system we landed on is blunt: every incident gets a runbook entry, no exceptions. A repeated page triggers a doc review. We delete stale docs as aggressively as we write new ones, and runbook quality sits inside our definition of done.

Documentation has a PR problem because the payoff is invisible until you measure it. Fewer 2 AM pages. Faster onboarding. An on-call rotation people don't dread.

Nobody gets promoted for writing runbooks, which says more about promotion criteria than about runbooks.

If your team is drowning in pages, write the runbook before you buy the tool.
L15:
Three years fully remote, then this year we went hybrid, two days in the office. Some of it went the way we hoped. Some of it cost us people I didn't want to lose.

Retention is better than it's been in two years. Onboarding is faster. Cross-team work feels easier.

And 2 senior people quit over the change. Trust took a real hit during the transition, and there are still days when the office is half empty and people rightly wonder why they commuted.

I've stopped believing there's a correct answer to remote versus hybrid. Every model has tradeoffs and every policy disappoints someone; the only variable you control is honesty. We told the team exactly why we made the change, and we accepted that some people would make a different call for their lives. I respect the two who did.

Anyone claiming this debate is settled is selling something.
L16:
AI won't replace junior developers. It's already changing what junior means, though.

We hired 2 juniors on my team recently. Both use AI pair-programming tools every day, and they ship production code faster than juniors did five years ago. By a lot. What's shifted is where their value comes from: less memorizing syntax and grinding out boilerplate, more reviewing code critically, asking better questions, and learning how systems fit together from day one.

Three consequences I believe. Hiring rubrics built on syntax trivia are obsolete. Mentorship matters more now, because judgment can't be autocompleted. And the ladder from junior to senior is compressing.

Companies that stop hiring juniors "because AI" aren't cutting a cost. They're cutting off their own senior pipeline.

Are you still hiring juniors?
L17:
A churned customer came back last week, on their own.

When they originally left, they told us why: seat-based pricing punished them for growing, and they were paying for licenses nobody used. So we switched to usage-based pricing. It was scary. We modeled the downside a dozen times, and a couple of advisors told us flatly not to do it.

Since the switch, expansion revenue is up 22%, sales conversations start with value instead of license counts, and churned customers have started returning unprompted.

Pricing is a statement about whose side you're on. Seat-based paid us when customers overbought. Usage-based pays us only when they succeed. Aligning incentives with your customers is good ethics that happens to be good business.
L18:
Six months ago a bootcamp grad asked me to mentor them. This week they signed an offer: frontend developer at an insurance company.

The work was theirs. What I supplied was structure: weekly check-ins even when progress felt slow, code reviews on real projects instead of toy exercises, 4 mock interviews that each got harder than the last, and some honest conversations about rejection along the way.

What surprised me is how little of mentoring is having answers. Most of it is showing up consistently while someone's confidence wobbles.

People love debating whether bootcamp grads can make it in this industry. From where I sit, the debate is settled. With support and stubbornness, yes.

If you've been a developer for a while, mentor someone; an hour a week can change a career.

To my mentee: congratulations. You earned all of it.
L19:
We changed one email subject line and open rates jumped 31%.

For months, every send to our 18k subscribers led with the feature, "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard," and the open rates were respectable, nothing special, the kind of numbers you stop checking. Then we rewrote the line to name the outcome instead: "Find out where your pipeline is leaking." Same email, same list, same send time.

Up 31%.

The principle is older than email marketing and we still needed the reminder. Readers don't care about your features; they care about what those features do for them. One line talks about you. The other talks about them.

We've since rewritten every subject line in our lifecycle emails the same way, and the gains have held.

Worth auditing your last ten sends: how many talk about you versus your reader?
L20:
Our 12-person team runs on 5 tools. One we built ourselves.

Linear holds every task and bug; if it's not in Linear, it doesn't exist. Notion is the company brain: docs, meeting notes, onboarding. Slack, with strict channel hygiene because the alternative is noise. Figma is where product ideas get real before anyone writes a line of code, and Otto, our homegrown deploy bot, takes a PR to production on one command. The team talks about Otto like a coworker.

That's the whole stack.

The principle behind the small number: every new tool charges a tax (context-switching, licenses, onboarding, integrations), and we only add one when the pain of not having it clearly beats that tax.

Simplicity is a competitive advantage. What's the one tool your team couldn't lose?
L21:
I took my first real break in 4 years. Two weeks, no Slack, no email, no quick calls.

The first few days were uncomfortable in a way I didn't expect. I kept checking my phone out of habit, feeling guilty about nothing in particular, half convinced things would fall apart without me. They didn't.

The useful part came after. I got back, looked at my calendar with two weeks of distance, and saw how much of my busyness was self-inflicted. I killed 3 recurring meetings in my first week back. Nobody has missed them.

Two things I believe now. Rest can't wait for the work to be finished, because the work is never finished. And if a business can't survive two weeks without its leader, that's a design flaw, not a badge of honor.

The sabbatical you think you can't afford is probably the one you need most.

When was your last real break?
L22:
Three years ago we were 4 people in a garage in Denver. This week we hired employee number 50.

I keep scrolling through old photos of that garage: the folding tables, the space heater, the whiteboard we bought off Craigslist. We serve 900 customers now, and the fifty still feels less believable than the nine hundred.

What I'm proudest of isn't the growth. It's that the values we scribbled on that Craigslist whiteboard still hold: customers first, default to transparency, hire people better than you.

To the first 4: you believed when there was nothing to point at. To the newest 46: you chose us anyway. To the 900 customers: everything we build is for you.

Back to work. There's plenty of it.
L23:
My last 3 clients all came from writing online. Zero came from networking events, and I used to go to all of them: conferences, mixers, founder happy hours. Hundreds of business cards collected, not one client to show for it.

Writing wins for structural reasons. A conversation reaches one person; a post reaches thousands, and it keeps working months after you hit publish, while a handshake is forgotten by Monday. Better still, the right people come to you already sold on how you think.

Networking events optimize for feeling productive. Writing optimizes for being findable.

Relationships still matter more than anything. The best ones just start when someone reads your ideas and thinks, this person gets it.

Stop collecting business cards. Publish your thinking instead. Your next client isn't at a conference; they're scrolling a feed.
L24:
I went on Supply Chain Weekly this week, episode 142, to talk about AI demand forecasting.

The number I kept coming back to on air: at one of our pilot customers, forecast error is down 18%. That isn't an abstract stat. Less error means less overstock, fewer stockouts, and working capital freed up from bad guesses.

We also spent real time on the unglamorous parts: data quality, change management, and why forecasting teams matter more with AI in the loop, not less. Traditional methods break down in volatile markets, and gluing a model onto a broken planning process fixes nothing. That was most of the conversation, honestly the part I enjoyed most.

The hosts asked sharp questions. Episode link is in the first comment if demand planning is your world.
L25:
Year in review, with the mistake left in.

ARR grew from $1.2M to $3.4M. The team went from 9 to 21. NPS is 61, and that's the number I care about most, because growth on top of customers who don't love the product is borrowed time.

The mistake: we hired sales reps too early, before we, the founders, had nailed the sales motion ourselves. Months of missed targets and frustrated reps followed, and none of it was their fault. You can't hand off a playbook you haven't written. We rebuilt the process from first principles and it finally clicked, but I'd take those months back if I could.

I'm sharing the ugly part because year-in-review posts are usually highlight reels, and growth is messier than the graphs suggest.

What did this year cost you that the metrics don't show?
